paper_title: LaLa-World: Scaling Latent World Models with Natural Language Actions

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: This paper shows that JEPA-style latent world models (LWMs) can learn across diverse domains and data sources by adopting the language-conditioned interface of video generation models. We establish this approach as an effective and efficient basis for planning with imagination and downstream policy fine-tuning. To this end, we introduce LaLa-World, a Language-conditioned Latent World model that learns from simulation and robot trajectories together with broader image and video data. Two designs make this work. First, we describe both numerical actions and visual changes in language, enabling joint training of a single future predictor across heterogeneous datasets. Second, we build the predictor on a language model, allowing it to interpret language conditions while predicting future latent states. The resulting predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than existing LWMs trained separately for each domain or task. Adding image and video data further improves average planning performance and robustness to action phrasing. In a matched comparison with an RAEv2-based video generation model baseline, LaLa-World reaches comparable planning performance with $6\times$ less training cost and $13.9\times$ faster planning. Beyond planning, the pretrained LaLa-World serves as an initialization for LaLa-Policy, which jointly predicts actions and future visual representations. LaLa-Policy performs competitively with Cosmos Policy on LIBERO and RoboCasa, with up to $5.5\times$ faster inference.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A central capability of an intelligent agent is to anticipate how the world will change in response to its actions. Before pushing cup across table, we know where it will end up and whether it might fall. World models capture this capability by predicting future states under candidate actions, providing basis for planning or decision-making (Sutton, 1991; Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; LeCun, 2022; Hafner et al., 2020). promising approach to making this predictive capability computationally efficient is to model how visual representations change under actions, without learning to reconstruct images at the pixel level. This motivates our focus on JEPA-style latent world models (LWMs), such as V-JEPA 2-AC (Assran et al., 2025) and DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025).1 This efficiency of LWMs is particularly useful for planning with imagination in the latent space, which requires repeatedly evaluating candidate action sequences, by rolling out multiple candidate futures at low cost (Hansen et al., 2022). However, despite this advantage, the action-conditioned predictors in such LWMs have largely been trained on simulation or robotics datasets, where numerical actions have domain-specific dimensions and physical meanings. For example, [2, 4] may encode horizontal and vertical displacement in one domain and [4] force in another, complicating the learning of shared dynamics. Furthermore, image and video data, which provide rich source of observations of the world, often lack these numerical action annotations, making them difficult to use for training action-conditioned future predictors. Therefore, scaling LWMs across diverse control actions and broader image and video data requires shared interface that accommodates heterogeneous data. We suggest that language can serve as the shared interface. We introduce LaLa-World, languageconditioned LWM that learns from diverse control datasets and broader image and video data with single future predictor. Language conditioning already supports learning from diverse visual data in video generation (Wan et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2025). We use language as shared interface for numerical actions and visual changes and can thereby scale LWM training with single predictor across diverse contexts and actions. As illustrated in Figure 1, LaLa-World has two main designs. First, we convert numerical actions in simulation or robotics datasets into natural language, allowing them to be expressed in the same form, such as move 2 left and 4 up and push with force 2 downward . We combine these control trajectories with image and video transitions described in language to help the predictor relate descriptions to visual changes across diverse scenes. Second, we equip the future predictor with language understanding. Built on language model, it interprets language conditions while predicting future latent states. These designs allow one model to learn from different action spaces and data sources through shared prediction objective. Figure 2 shows that single LaLa-World predictor serves multiple domains and predicts future states under qualitative actions such as move slightly left . 1Throughout this paper, LWMs refer to JEPA-style world models trained without DreamerV3s reconstruction loss (Hafner et al., 2025a) or TD-MPC2s reward supervision (Hansen et al., 2024). 3 Figure 2: MPC planning with language actions. LaLa-World imagines future representations under candidate actions with MPC and selects the most promising action toward the goal. Because all actions share one language interface, single LaLa-World predictor can plan across multiple domains, despite differences in action dimensionality and physical meaning. The predictor also supports language-based actions without numerical values (bottom two rows), as detailed in Section D.4.3. The visualized observations result from executing the selected actions in the simulator. Our experiments show that our jointly trained predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than existing LWM baselines trained separately for each domain. We also show that adding image and video data to training further improves planning performance and robustness to action phrasing. We compare LaLa-World with an RAEv2-based generative world model (Singh et al., 2026), whose predictor uses diffusion Transformer (DiT). With the same language conditions, training data, and visual encoder, LaLa-World outperforms this RAEv2 baseline in planning with 6 less training cost and 13.9 faster inference. Beyond planning, we investigate whether the pretrained LWM can serve as useful initialization for policy fine-tuning. Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., 2026) demonstrates this use of pretrained video model by adapting Cosmos-Predict2 (Ali et al., 2025) to predict robot actions together with future frames. Similarly, we fine-tune LaLa-World into LaLa-Policy for joint prediction of actions and future visual representations. On LIBERO and RoboCasa, LaLa-Policy performs competitively with Cosmos Policy while reducing average inference time per trajectory by factor of up to 5.5. We hope these results draw greater attention to latent world models, showing that even without visually compelling outputs, they can offer practical advantages over generative world models in planning and downstream policy learning. We summarize our contributions as follows: We introduce LaLa-World, latent world model that uses language as shared interface for joint training on control trajectories and broader image and video data. We show that single LaLa-World predictor learns dynamics across domains and outperforms existing LWMs in MPC planning. We compare LaLa-World with an RAEv2-based generative world model under matched settings, demonstrating higher planning performance and greater training and inference efficiency. We fine-tune the pretrained LaLa-World into LaLa-Policy, which performs competitively with existing policy models while achieving faster inference than Cosmos Policy. 4 Figure 3: Examples of language-conditioned transition data. Each example consists of past observations, language condition, and the next observation. Language conditions describe either numerical control actions from simulation and robotics or visual changes in images and videos. This shared interface enables training single LWM across different action spaces and data sources.

sections.title: 2 Background and Motivation
sections.content: World models aim to predict how an environment evolves under given condition (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; LeCun, 2022; Wan et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2025). One approach to making future prediction computationally efficient is to predict changes in latent representations. Latent World Models (LWMs), including V-JEPA 2-AC (Assran et al., 2025) and DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025), follow this approach. These models commonly use numerical actions in the following action-conditioned formulation: et = Eθ(xt), (1) where xt and ct denote the observation and k-dimensional numerical action condition at time t, respectively, Eθ encodes observations into latent representations, and Pϕ predicts the future latent ˆet+1 from context window of length w. The action-conditioned predictors in these models are commonly trained on simulation or robotics trajectories and evaluated through planning in domain-specific manner (Sobal et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026a;b) ˆet+1 = Pϕ (etw+1:t, ctw+1:t) , ct Rk, Video generation models (i.e., generative world models) are trained to synthesize images or videos conditioned on language (Brooks et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2025). This language interface allows them to learn visual changes across domains and data sources. Through this training, these models acquire world knowledge that extends their capabilities beyond video generation. Their pretrained weights, for instance, serve as prior for action prediction: Cosmos Policy fine-tunes Cosmos-Predict2 into robot policy (Kim et al., 2026; Ali et al., 2025). For LWMs, however, learning jointly from heterogeneous control datasets and broader visual data remains underexplored, as does their use in downstream policy learning. We therefore explore an approach that retains the efficiency of LWMs while adopting the flexible language interface of generative world models. The resulting model supports evaluation against existing LWMs in planning and against generative world models in both planning and policy fine-tuning.

sections.title: 3 LaLa-World
sections.content: We introduce LaLa-World, Language-conditioned Latent World model whose predictor takes language condition instead of the numerical action condition in Equation (1). Two components are needed: transition data that describes the change from xt to xt+1 in language, and predictor that understands it. Section 3.1 covers the first, describing how we construct such language-conditioned data, and Section 3.2 covers the second with the architecture and training objective.

sections.title: 3.1 Language-Conditioned Transition Data
sections.content: Language unifies the action spaces of multiple domains. Simulation and robotics datasets used to train LWMs record actions as numerical vectors. We convert these vectors into language 5 conditions using fixed templates, as illustrated in Figure 3, retaining each domains numerical values with their direction and magnitude. Language thus expresses actions across domains in common form, allowing their control data to be pooled to train single predictor. We apply this conversion to seven simulation and robotics datasets described in Section 4. The actions in these domains may differ in physical meaning and dimensionality. This raises the key question of whether single future predictor can learn dynamics across these domains. Details of the dataset composition and conversion templates are provided in Section D.1. Language enables action-conditioned training on broader image and video data. We also train the same future predictor on image and video transitions without numerical action annotations, using descriptions of visual change as conditions. Such data matter because the converted control datasets describe actions with fixed templates, which exposes the predictor to only narrow range of language. In addition, descriptions of visual change provide language conditions for these transitions, extending training beyond the control trajectories. We therefore supplement them with captioned videos from OpenVid (Nan et al., 2025) and image-editing pairs with instructions from OmniEdit (Wei et al., 2025) and ShareGPT (Chen et al., 2025b). In these data, the caption describing the change between frames or the editing instruction serves directly as the language condition, so no numerical action annotation is needed. The predictor thereby sees wider range of language and visual change.

sections.title: 3.2 Model Architecture and Objective
sections.content: As shown in Figure 1(b), LaLa-World follows the encoder-predictor framework of existing LWMs, with simple adaptations for language conditioning. Below, we describe the observation encoder (i.e., vision encoder), transition predictor (i.e., future predictor), and training objective. Encoder. LWMs use an observation encoder to map each RGB frame xt to latent representation et (Assran et al., 2025; Terver et al., 2025). For this role, vision transformers pretrained with self-supervised objectives are commonly used, including DINO encoders (Oquab et al., 2024; Siméoni et al., 2025) and V-JEPA 2 encoder (Assran et al., 2025). These encoders are pretrained on large collections of unlabeled images and videos, providing visual representations for diverse environments (Zhou et al., 2025). In V-JEPA 2-AC, the encoder remains frozen during world model training, which prevents encoder collapse and preserves its pretrained visual representations. Following JEPA-WMs (Terver et al., 2025), we use DINOv2-S/14 or DINOv3-L/16 as the frozen observation encoder. More details and ablations on vision encoders are provided in Section C.5. Predictor. The predictor Pϕ takes the visual context etw+1:t and the language condition as input and predicts the next latent representation ˆet+1. Existing world models typically receive conditions in two ways: LWMs incorporate numerical actions through mechanisms such as AdaLN (Terver et al., 2025), feature conditioning (Zhou et al., 2025), and sequence conditioning (Nam et al., 2026), all of which offer no way to read text. Video generation models support language conditioning through separate text encoder whose outputs condition the predictor (Wan et al., 2025), which adds parameters and text-encoding cost. LaLa-World addresses both limitations by using pretrained language model as the predictor itself: it reads the language condition as text and predicts future latent representations in the same network. Specifically, we use Qwen3.5-0.8B (Qwen Team, 2026) as our default predictor backbone. The language condition is tokenized using the models tokenizer and mapped to token embeddings, which are passed to the predictor together with the visual latents. To map the visual latents into the same embedding space, we use two-layer MLP and add 3D positional embeddings indexed by time and 2D spatial location (Wang et al., 2024). The output ˆet+1 is then read out from learned query tokens (Pan et al., 2025). We train the predictor by minimizing the squared error between the predicted and target future representations: = ˆet+1 et+12. Notably, we use proprioceptive state neither as an input nor as prediction target. While proprioception can benefit LWMs tailored to specific domain, it is defined in domain-specific manner, which limits its applicability to domain-agnostic world model. We further examine the predictors backbone and architectural choices through ablations in Section C.3 and D.2, respectively, including BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and Gemma (Gemma Team, 2025) as alternative backbones. sections.title: 4 MPC Planning
sections.content: Suppose we want to move cup from our hand onto table while avoiding nearby objects. We imagine the outcomes of candidate action sequences and select the one that brings the cup closest to the desired position (i.e., planning with imagination). In robot planning, the world model provides these imagined outcomes: given an initial observation xinit and goal observation xgoal, planner selects the action sequence whose imagined outcome is closest to the goal. Following prior LWM studies (Zhou et al., 2025; Terver et al., 2025), we evaluate planning with model predictive control (MPC), using the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) to optimize action sequences (Rubinstein, 1997). Evaluation Setup. At each planning round, we sample candidate action sequences and, for each sequence, apply Equation (1) autoregressively for steps and score it by the squared distance between the final predicted latent state and the encoded goal: = ˆet+H egoal2 , egoal = Eθ(xgoal). (2) CEM repeatedly samples sequences and updates the sampling distribution using those with the lowest costs. For LaLa-World, we verbalize candidate actions using the training templates. In simulation, we execute the corresponding numerical actions from an initial segment of the selected sequence. For domains requiring re-planning, we obtain new observation and repeat this process. Benchmark-specific settings and evaluation criteria are provided in Section D.4. We use seven control datasets from DINO-WM and JEPA-WMs (Terver et al., 2025): six simulation datasetsWall (Zhou et al., 2025), PointMaze (Fu et al., 2020), Push-T (Chi et al., 2023), MetaWorld (Yu et al., 2020), Rope and Granular (Zhang et al., 2024)and the real-robot dataset DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024). We also evaluate on RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024), domain excluded from training, to assess zero-shot transfer. In addition to existing LWM baselines including DINO-WM, we also train the world models of IRIS (Micheli et al., 2023), DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., 2025a), and TD-MPC2 (Hansen et al., 2024) on the same control datasets without reward or task information, which is the same setup for these baselines in DINO-WM. For fair comparison, we train each baseline using its public implementation on the same data and evaluate all under the same planning settings, including horizon and none uses proprioceptive states. Decoder. To visualize and interpret predicted futures, we build 12-layer transformer decoder that maps predicted latents to RGB images: ˆxt+1 = D(ˆet+1). We train the decoder with combination of L1 reconstruction and LPIPS perceptual losses (Zhang et al., 2018), following the decoder training recipe of RAEv2 (Singh et al., 2026). It should be noted that the decoder is not used during world model training (Section 3.2). 7 4.1 Results and Analysis jointly trained LaLa-World predictor performs well across diverse domains. Table 1 reports MPC planning results across simulation and robot domains. While existing LWMs are typically trained within individual domains, LaLa-World trains its predictor jointly across all domains with different action spaces and physical dynamics. Despite these differences, LaLa-World achieves the highest average score in both benchmark groups in Table 1. On the five simulation tasks in the upper table, LaLa-World reaches an average success rate of 72.1%, exceeding JEPA-WMs by 7.5 percentage points. The largest gain over the best baseline in this group is on Push-T, where success increases from 68.8% to 81.2%. LaLa-World also achieves the highest zero-shot success rates on both RoboCasa tasks, reaching 40.6% on Reach and 46.9% on Place. Training on image and video data improves performance and robustness to phrasing. We evaluate the effect of training LaLa-World on image and video transitions and find two benefits. The results are shown in Figure 4. First, adding image and video transitions improves planning performance. Specifically, the average score increases from 59.3 with control trajectories alone to 61.6 with all data. Second, LaLa-World becomes more robust when the same actions are expressed in different words. To evaluate this, we paraphrase the action templates at evaluation, for example, replacing move the gripper with shift the robot hand and move the agent with push the dot . LaLa-World remains robust when trained on all data, including image and video transitions, whereas paraphrasing lowers the average score by 6.8 points with control trajectories alone. Further details and domain-level results are provided in Section C.7. Fig. 4: Benefits of image /video data inclusion. LaLa-World can predict the future from language without numbers. The language actions in our control trajectories retain numerical magnitudes. We next ask whether LaLa-World can predict outcomes from qualitative descriptions such as move slightly down . Using the action ranges observed in the training data, we define conversion function that replaces each numerical magnitude with one of three qualitative levels: slightly, no modifier, or far. CEM samples numerical action sequences as before and passes them through this function to obtain the language conditions for LaLa-World. The bottom two rows of Figure 2 show successful planning examples in Wall and RoboCasa under these conditions. These examples indicate that the predictor can use qualitative descriptions to guide planning even when exact action magnitudes are unspecified. We provide more details on the evaluation setup in Section D.4.3 and additional results in Section C.6.

sections.title: 4.2 Latent vs. Generative World Models
sections.content: With language as the action interface, LaLa-World can be compared with generative world models trained on the same kinds of data. LWMs learn to match future visual latents, whereas generative world models are trained for pixel-level generation. We ask how these approaches compare in planning performance and computational cost. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comparison of latent and generative world models in planning under matched conditions, including language conditions and training data, as discussed in Section A.2. Setup for matched comparison. We use RAEv2 (Singh et al., 2026) as our generative world model baseline because it uses DINOv3-L/16 (Siméoni et al., 2025) rather than VAE as its vision encoder. LaLa-World uses the same encoder in this comparison. Both models use language as the action interface and receive the same language conditions. We train both models on the same control trajectories and image and video transitions used to train LaLa-World. The full-depth predictors are comparable in size: LaLa-Worlds predictor and RAEv2s DiT (Peebles & Xie, 2023) each contain approximately 0.8B parameters. We initialize RAEv2 from its publicly released pretrained DiT weights and follow its training implementation, including flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023) and REPA (Yu et al., 2025). During planning, we use one or five denoising steps per prediction and compute the cost in Equation (2) between the resulting future representations and the encoded goal. Further details of RAEv2 are provided in Section D.5. We compare the two world models in terms of training cost and planning time. sections.title: 5 LaLa-Policy: From World Model To Action Predictor
sections.content: We now ask whether this pretrained LaLa-World provides useful initialization for policy finetuning. Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., 2026) takes this approach by fine-tuning the pretrained video generation model Cosmos-Predict2 (Ali et al., 2025) to jointly predict actions and future frames. LaLa-Policy. Following Cosmos Policys fine-tuning procedure, we fine-tune LaLa-World into LaLa-Policy using policy data to predict an action chunk together with future latent representation. We add learned action queries to the predictor Pϕ alongside its queries for future prediction. Given an observation xt and task instruction ℓ, the outputs at the action queries provide sequence of conditioning features ht:t+N 1 for an action generator Aψ built on diffusion transformer. We use the action-head architecture of Isaac-GR00T (Bjorck et al., 2025), which conditions action generation on vision-language features. Starting from Gaussian noise, Aψ generates the action chunk through iterative denoising: (ˆet+N , ht:t+N 1) = Pϕ (Eθ(xt), ℓ) , ˆat:t+N 1 = Aψ (ϵ; ht:t+N 1) , ϵ (0, I). (3) Here, is the number of actions in the chunk, and the future prediction targets Eθ(xt+N ). Modeling an action distribution allows the policy to represent multiple action sequences for reaching the goal. Policy fine-tuning setup. We compare LaLa-Policy with policies that predict actions alone (Intelligence et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b) and models that jointly predict actions and future observations (Li et al., 2025a; Liang et al., 2025). For fair comparison with the joint prediction baselines, we fine-tune Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., 2026) to predict only actions and future observations, without auxiliary future proprioception or value prediction. LaLa-Policy follows the same prediction setup in latent space. We fine-tune on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) and RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024), using demonstration trajectories composed of transitions (xt, at, xt+1) and paired with task instructions. For RoboCasa, we consider two training sets: 50 human demonstrations or 300 demonstrations generated with MimicGen per task. For LaLa-Policy, we keep the observation encoder frozen and jointly train the pretrained predictor and newly added policy modules. The action generator is trained from scratch. Dataset and training details are provided in Sections D.7 and D.8. Evaluation Setup. The policy models are evaluated in LIBERO and RoboCasa simulators. At each step, we execute 16 predicted actions on LIBERO and the first 16 of the 32 predicted actions on RoboCasa. We report success rates, counting trial as successful only if it meets the simulators task-specific success criterion within the allowed number of actions. More details are in Section D.9 LaLa-Policy achieves competitive and efficient action prediction via latent world modeling. Tables 2 and 3 show that LaLa-World can be fine-tuned into an effective policy, performing competitively with Cosmos Policy on both benchmarks. Notably, this performance comes with up to 5.5 faster inference, measured by average inference time per trajectory  (Table 4)  . Since LaLaPolicy is not trained for pixel reconstruction, decoded images may contain visual inaccuracies. these findings suggest that effective world models and action predictors can be learned without pixel reconstruction objective. World modeling pretraining also benefits policy fine-tuning. Initializing the predictor from LaLa-World outperforms both random and Qwen3.5 initialization on both LIBERO and RoboCasa. This agrees with the finding of Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., 2026) that Cosmos-Predict2, pretrained on diverse videos, provides useful prior for policy learning, and extends this observation to latent world models. LaLa-Policy can anticipate future latent states resulting from its predicted actions. Given the current observation and task instruction, LaLa-Policy jointly predicts an action chunk and future latent representation. During policy execution in LIBERO and RoboCasa, we decode the predicted representations into images and visualize them alongside simulator observations in Figure 7. The decoded futures capture both robot motion and changes in object position during lifting and transport, showing that latent prediction can represent the dynamics of manipulation.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented LaLa-World, latent world model that learns from heterogeneous control trajectories and broader image and video data through shared language interface. This enables comparisons with existing LWMs in MPC planning and generative models in planning and policy fine-tuning. Despite sharing one predictor across domains, LaLa-World outperforms existing LWMs in average MPC planning performance. Under matched settings, including training data, it also surpasses the generative baseline in planning performance and efficiency. Following Cosmos Policys use of world models pretrained on diverse data for policy learning, we fine-tuned LaLa-World into LaLa-Policy. It outperforms evaluated VLA baselines and achieves substantially faster inference than Cosmos Policy. These results demonstrate the value of latent world models for planning and policy learning without training to reconstruct visual details. We hope this work draws greater attention to latent world models, their scalability, and downstream uses. For broader practical impact, future work could explore scaling training data and model size, extending prediction horizons, and evaluating policies on real robots, as discussed in Section B. 11 Acknowledgments We gratefully acknowledge NAVER AI Lab for providing the resources and support that facilitated this research. sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: We summarize in Figure how LaLa-World and LaLa-Policy compare with representative world models and policy models. Figure A: Comparison with representative world models and policy models. (a) LaLa-World uses natural language conditions, enabling training on control trajectories together with image and video transitions. The RAEv2-based WM is our generative world model baseline under matched settings in Section 4.2. (b) Fine-tuned from LaLa-World, LaLa-Policy jointly predicts actions and future latents, whereas VLAs predict actions alone and Cosmos Policy predicts actions and the future with visual details. A.1 Latent World Models Latent world models predict future states in learned representation space rather than in pixels. Recent work follows the joint-embedding predictive architecture (Assran et al., 2023; 2025). Existing studies focus on improving latent prediction for planning (Assran et al., 2025) or stabilizing training (Maes et al., 2026a). In the former direction, PLDM (Sobal et al., 2025) demonstrates reward-free planning with learned latent dynamics, while DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025) shows the effectiveness of using frozen DINOv2 vision encoder. V-JEPA 2-AC (Assran et al., 2025) extends latent planning to real-robot manipulation, and JEPA-WMs (Terver et al., 2025) study design choices including multistep rollouts. An orthogonal direction addresses training stability: LeWorldModel (Maes et al., 2026a) trains the vision encoder and predictor end to end, using SIGReg to prevent representation collapse. AdaJEPA (Wang et al., 2026) further improves robustness by updating the predictor at test time. These methods typically train action-conditioned predictors within single domain, limiting their development into General World Models. Although Newt (Hansen et al., 2025) learns across multiple domains, its training remains focused on control and game environments. Joint training of action-conditioned predictors on control trajectories and broader image and video transitions remains underexplored. We therefore use language to unify actions across control datasets and co-train them with diverse image and video transitions. Our use of language as the action interface differs from Dynalang (Lin et al., 2024), which incorporates language as observations or task descriptions. A.2 Video Generation Models Video generation models (i.e., generative world models) predict future observations conditioned on language (Ho et al., 2022; Blattmann et al., 2023b; Villegas et al., 2023; Kondratyuk et al., 2024). Language conditioning lets them learn from web-scale video (Brooks et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025), 17 and the resulting models serve as interactive simulators for games (Bruce et al., 2024), driving (Hu et al., 2023), and robotics (Yang et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2025; Ali et al., 2025). While video generation models can produce visually compelling content, using them for MPC planning is costly because evaluating candidate action sequences requires repeatedly synthesizing the future with visual details. V-JEPA 2-AC and V-JEPA 2.1 (Assran et al., 2025; Mur-Labadia et al., 2026) report faster planning than video generation baselines (Agarwal et al., 2025; Bar et al., 2025), but these comparisons differ in action interface, encoder, predictor size, and training data. RAE (Zheng et al., 2026; Singh et al., 2026) replaces the VAE encoder (Kingma & Welling, 2013) with vision encoder pretrained with self-supervision, allowing generative world model to share its encoder with an LWM. Using RAEv2 as generative world model baseline, we compare it with LaLa-World under matched settings, including language conditioning. A.3 Planning and Policy Learning with World Models Planning with learned dynamics models has long history (Sutton, 1991; Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Watter et al., 2015; Finn & Levine, 2017; Ebert et al., 2018). PlaNet (Hafner et al., 2019) plans with the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) in latent space trained with reconstruction and reward prediction. Dreamer (Hafner et al., 2020; 2021; 2025a;b) and IRIS (Micheli et al., 2023) instead train actor-critic policies on imagined rollouts. MuZero (Schrittwieser et al., 2020) and TD-MPC (Hansen et al., 2022; 2024) learn latent dynamics with reward and value prediction to support tree search and model predictive control, respectively. More recent work defines world model more narrowly as predictor of future states (Sobal et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026a). Planning with them is performed at test time by sampling-based optimization toward goal image (i.e., MPC planning). Our experiments follow this reward-free and goal-conditioned protocol. A.4 Action Prediction Models Vision-language-action (VLA) models such as RT-2 (Brohan et al., 2023), OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024), π0.5 (Intelligence et al., 2025), UniVLA (Bu et al., 2025), and CogVLA (Li et al., 2025b) fine-tune vision-language models on large-scale robot demonstrations to map an observation and an instruction to actions. These models predict actions alone. When humans want to move cup, however, they can imagine the action, how the cup will move, and where it will end up. Video-based policies such as UniPi (Du et al., 2023) and AVDC (Ko et al., 2024) first generate videos of task execution and then translate them into control actions. Unified video-action models (Li et al., 2025a; Zhu et al., 2025) instead predict actions and future frames jointly. Building on pretrained video models, Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., 2026) fine-tunes Cosmos-Predict2 (Ali et al., 2025) to jointly predict actions, future states, and values. LaLa-Policy follows this recipe but starts from latent world model, predicting future representations rather than reconstructing visual details. A.5 Visual Representation Pretraining Self-supervised visual encoders provide the representations on which latent world models learn dynamics (Zhou et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025). Contrastive and self-distillation methods (He et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Caron et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2024; Siméoni et al., 2025) learn invariances across augmented views, masked image modeling (He et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022) predicts masked patches, and JEPAs (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024) predict the representations of masked regions instead of their pixels. These encoders are conventionally evaluated by probing or fine-tuning on recognition tasks such as classification, segmentation, and depth estimation. V-JEPA 2 (Assran et al., 2025) introduced planning as further evaluation: the pretrained encoder is frozen, an actionconditioned predictor is trained on top of it from robot trajectories, and the pair is used for MPC planning toward image goals. We follow the same evaluation protocol as V-JEPA 2, DINO-WM, and JEPA-WMs (Terver et al., 2025).

sections.title: B Future Directions
sections.content: LaLa-World shows that shared language interface enables joint LWM training on heterogeneous control trajectories and broader image and video data, with benefits for planning and policy finetuning. These results suggest several directions for extending the current approach. 1. Scaling data and model capacity. With 0.8B predictor, adding image and video data improves planning performance and robustness to action phrasing (Figure 4). However, our training data remain smaller in scale than those of video generation models such as Wan (Wan et al., 2025), and we have not established whether these gains continue at larger scales. Future work should increase dataset size and predictor capacity separately and together, measuring their effects on planning performance and downstream policy learning. 2. Learning visual representations end to end. We freeze the vision encoder to prevent representation collapse, but this also prevents its representations from adapting to future prediction. Better world models may require visual representations that capture information useful for anticipating future states. Jointly training the vision encoder and predictor while preventing collapse is therefore an important direction for future work. 3. Extending prediction beyond one step. Video generation models produce sequences of future frames, whereas our predictor is trained with supervision only on the next latent state. Whether latent world models can learn to generate similarly long sequences through autoregressive prediction remains an open question. Addressing this would require training on autoregressive rollouts with losses over multiple future states, rather than only the next state. We leave this investigation to future work because of the additional training cost, with particular interest in how prediction quality changes as the rollout length increases. 4. Extending prediction horizons. Following the evaluation protocols of JEPA-WMs and DINOWM (Terver et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025), our MPC experiments use relatively short planning horizons of at most six steps (Table H). Evaluating longer horizons would help assess whether the model can anticipate distant consequences and support planning in real-world tasks that require such foresight. The multi-step supervision discussed above could support this extension. 5. Evaluating on real robots. Our experiments on LIBERO and RoboCasa show that initializing LaLa-Policy from LaLa-World outperforms existing VLAs, demonstrating the value of pretrained latent world model for policy fine-tuning. While these simulation experiments establish this benefit, extending the evaluation to real robots is an important next step. 6. Best-of-N planning with LaLa-Policy. LaLa-Policy achieves competitive action prediction without value supervision. Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., 2026) further learns from policy rollouts to predict future states and values for candidate action chunks, enabling best-of-N planning. We consider extending LaLa-Policy to such planning valuable avenue for future work. We hope these directions broaden the use of LWMs while retaining their efficiency in planning and policy learning.

sections.content: D.1 LaLa-World Training Data Details Table reports the training data size for each dataset. We combine these datasets and sample in proportion to their sizes. We reserve approximately 2% of episodes or editing pairs for validation and keep sequences from the same source video in one split. 26 Dataset Wall PointMaze Push-T MetaWorld Rope Granular DROID OpenVid-1M OmniEdit ShareGPT-4o-Image Training data size 86,296 186,675 2,199,488 1,162,310 18,525 18,582 1,500,000 1,023,363 295,353 45,613 Table G: Data used to train LaLa-World. We count target transitions for control and video data and editing pairs for OmniEdit and ShareGPT-4o-Image. Counts exclude validation data and count each control transition once across its two action description formats. Simulation data. We use the six simulation datasets from DINO-WM and JEPA-WMs (Zhou et al., 2025; Terver et al., 2025) listed in Section 4. For Wall, PointMaze, Push-T, and MetaWorld, each transition spans five simulator steps; for Rope and Granular, it spans one push. We enumerate overlapping transitions within each episode and pair each with both numerical and qualitative action descriptions. Action aggregation is described in Section D.4.2. DROID. We use the LeRobot release of DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024), retaining one external camera view and every fourth frame of the 15-fps recordings.3 We derive action descriptions from changes in end-effector position, orientation, and gripper state between retained frames. Our DROID subset contains 1.5 million target transitions, approximately 20% of the original datasets transitions. This keeps DROID from dominating the mixture under fixed training budget. The same subset is used for both action description formats. Image and video data. From OpenVid-1M (Nan et al., 2025), we select clips by duration, motion, and aesthetic scores and extract ten-frame sequences at 0.5-second intervals. Qwen3-VL-30BA3B-Instruct describes the visible change between each adjacent frame pair to provide its language condition. We also use sourceedited image pairs and their instructions from OmniEdit (Wei et al., 2025) and ShareGPT-4o-Image (Chen et al., 2025b). Further DROID-focused post-training, as in V-JEPA 2-AC (Assran et al., 2025), may improve robot planning; we leave this to future work. D.2 LaLa-World Architecture Details Each example contains observed context frames, language conditions for the corresponding transitions, and one target frame. In multi-frame training, we sample the context length uniformly from one to three frames, subject to the available episode history; image pairs provide one context frame. two-layer MLP projects each frames patch representations into the language models embedding space. As illustrated in Figure G(a), we append one query token per target patch after the context and language tokens. The queries are copies of shared learned vector, with their target locations specified by 3D positional embeddings. These embeddings encode temporal index and the row and column of each spatial patch. Context patches share temporal index within each frame, while queries receive the target frames temporal index and spatial coordinates. We concatenate sinusoidal encodings for the three axes, multiply them by learnable scale, and add them to the input embeddings while retaining the backbones native positional encoding. The appended queries receive the preceding visual and language context through the LLM backbone. two-layer MLP prediction head maps their output hidden states back to the vision encoders feature dimension, producing the future patch grid in one forward pass. Both projection MLPs use GELU between their linear layers. Position and angle errors are measured at the final step, using L2 distance for position. DROID is evaluated offline without simulator execution. D.3 LaLa-World Training Details We keep the observation encoder frozen and jointly train the language-model backbone, visual projection layers, and learned query tokens. The same encoder provides the context and target representations. We optimize the prediction objective in Section 3.2. We use AdamW with an effective global batch size of 512, (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.98), and weight decay of 0.05. The learning rate increases linearly from 1 105 to 2 104 over the first 1,000 optimizer steps, followed by cosine decay schedule with minimum learning rate of 1 106. We clip the gradient norm at 1.0 and use gradient accumulation to maintain the global batch size. We train for 20 epochs using bfloat16 mixed precision on eight NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs. We define each epoch as approximately one million training examples sampled from the training pool. D.4 MPC Planning and Evaluation Details D.4.1 Benchmark Settings and Evaluation Metrics We follow the planning and evaluation protocols of JEPA-WMs (Terver et al., 2025) and DINOWM (Zhou et al., 2025), with our own success criteria for Rope and Granular. As in Section 4, we evaluate planning with model predictive control (MPC), using the cross-entropy method (CEM) to optimize action sequences. Table summarizes the MPC settings, CEM parameters, and evaluation criteria for each benchmark. One planning step corresponds to one transition predicted by the world model. In simulation, each action update within step is called substep. The planning horizon specifies how many steps the model predicts ahead during each candidate rollout, while trajectory length gives the total step budget. In simulation, we execute an initial segment of the sequence optimized by CEM, whose length is specified by executed steps. For benchmarks requiring replanning, we follow the MPC loop: after executing this segment, we obtain new observation and re-optimize the action sequence with CEM. Figure illustrates these settings. Wall executes all six planned steps in one round, whereas MetaWorld Reach executes three of six and Rope and Granular execute one of five before replanning. For DROID, we evaluate planned actions offline without simulator execution. We compute the endpoint position error errorxyz in meters from the cumulative planned displacement and report the Action Score: Action Score = max (0, 800 (0.1 errorxyz)) . For zero-shot planning on RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024), we reuse DROIDs action sampling statistics because the two domains share the same action definitions and dimensionality. Yet, it is notable that LaLa-World achieves accurate prediction and high planning success rates. D.4.2 Action Aggregation and Execution The baselines represent each planning step by concatenating the actions across its substeps. For example, five substeps with two action components, and y, yield 10-dimensional vector. Verbalizing every component would produce long language condition. We therefore sum each component across substeps when constructing the training data and verbalize only these sums. In this example, the language condition describes two values, = (cid:80)5 i=1 yi, as shown in Figure J(a). i=1 xi and = (cid:80)5 Within MPC, CEM optimizes action sequences in this aggregated action space, with its initial sampling statistics computed from the aggregated training data. Each sampled action is verbalized using the training templates to condition the predictor. To execute selected action, we divide each optimized sum by the number of substeps and repeat the resulting action at every substep. For the five-substep example, we apply (x/5, y/5) five times, as illustrated in Figure J(b). This preserves the component sums but discards variation within step, which can lead to differences between predicted and executed transitions. It is notable that LaLa-World achieves accurate future prediction and high planning success rates despite this loss of information. D.4.3 Qualitative Language Action Conversion Figure illustrates the conversion rule and the planning procedure. Action conversion. Numerical language actions preserve each action components direction and magnitude. To construct qualitative descriptions, we define conversion rule for each component and direction using the action range observed in the corresponding training data. We divide the interval from zero to the maximum observed magnitude into three equal-width bins, represented by slightly, no modifier, and far, respectively. The direction remains unchanged. For example, when the 29 (a) Action conversion Numerical language action Leftward magnitude in training data Qualitative language action move 0.4 left move 3.0 left move 4.5 left slightly no modiﬁer far 0 2 4 move slightly left move left move far left 6: maximum observed magnitude 6 (b) MPC planning procedure Costs update the sampling distribution CEM samples numerical actions move 4.5 left Conversion rule from (a) move far left LaLa-World latent rollout Predicted latents Goal-distance cost Selected actions keep their numerical values: move 4.5 left Current and goal observations Next observation; replan Simulator execution Figure K: MPC planning with qualitative language actions. (a) Each magnitude maps to one of three equal-width bins, and the direction is kept. (b) LaLa-World evaluates CEM samples through their qualitative descriptions, while the simulator executes the selected actions with their numerical values. Thus, LaLa-World plans without exact action magnitudes. maximum leftward magnitude is 6, move 0.4 left becomes move slightly left , and move 4.5 left becomes move far left . MPC planning procedure. At each MPC planning round, CEM samples numerical action sequences as in the main experiments. Before each sequence is evaluated by LaLa-World, the conversion rule maps its actions to qualitative descriptions. These descriptions condition the latent rollout, which CEM scores using the same goal-distance cost in Equation (2). The simulator executes the selected actions using their original numerical values, and re-planning follows the same MPC procedure. We keep the trained predictor and all other planning settings unchanged. D.5 RAEv2 Baseline Details Model and initialization. We initialize the generative world model baselines DiT from the released RAEv2 checkpoint pretrained for image generation on ImageNet.4 Its frozen DINOv3-L/16 encoder aggregates features from seven layers to form the visual representation et = Eθ(xt). frozen Qwen3-0.6B encodes the language condition into text embeddings (z). Training. For each transition (xt, z, xt+1), we encode the future observation as et+1 = Eθ(xt+1) and interpolate it with Gaussian noise for flow matching (Singh et al., 2026): e(τ ) t+1 = (1 τ )et+1 + τ ϵ, ϵ (0, I), τ [0, 1]. (6) Here, indexes environment time and τ denotes the noise level. The DiT receives e(τ ) t+1, τ , the current observation representation et, and the text embeddings (z). We train it with flow matching and representation alignment (REPA) loss (Yu et al., 2025) that aligns intermediate DiT features with DINOv2-B/14 features of the future observation. MPC planning. We use the same MPC procedure as LaLa-World, with CEM optimizing candidate action sequences. Starting from Gaussian noise, the DiT produces future representation ˆet+1 through denoising, conditioned on the current observation and language action. We evaluate RAEv2 with one and five denoising steps per prediction. CEM scores candidate action sequences using the mean squared error between the final predicted representation ˆet+H and the encoded goal Eθ(xgoal), following Equation (2). The goal is encoded with the same DINOv3-L/16 feature aggregation as the training targets. Pixel decoding is not used to compute the planning cost. 4https://huggingface.co/nyu-visionx/RAEv2-models/tree/main/stage2/imagenet/ dinov3l-k7 Encoded observations ht:t+N 1 Gaussian noise ϵ Task instruction Action queries Future queries Predictor Pϕ ﬁne-tuned from LaLa-World Action generator Aψ ˆat ˆat+N Action chunk Future latents ˆet+N Figure L: LaLa-Policy architecture. The predictor, fine-tuned from LaLa-World, receives encoded observations, task instruction, and learned action and future queries. It predicts future visual latents and provides conditioning features for an action generator, which produces an action chunk from Gaussian noise. Proprio and intermediate projections are omitted for clarity. Visualization. For Figure 6, RAEv2s predicted representations are mapped to pixels with its released DINOv3-L-K7 decoder,5 while LaLa-World uses the decoder described in Section 4. D.6 LaLa-Policy Architecture Details As illustrated in Figure L, LaLa-Policy extends the predictor of LaLa-World with proprioceptive input and action queries. Following previous VLAs that use SigLIP-based visual encoders (Black et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b), we use SigLIP2-So400M/14 at 224 224 resolution and the 24-layer Qwen3.5-0.8B as the predictor backbone. Each camera view is encoded independently, and shared two-layer MLP projects its patch representations into the backbones embedding space. We add learned view embeddings and map the current proprioceptive state to one token through separate MLP. The input sequence contains visual tokens, the proprioceptive token, task instruction tokens, action queries, and future queries, in this order. We use = 16 action queries for LIBERO and = 32 for RoboCasa, with one future query per spatial patch in each camera view. two-layer MLP maps the future-query outputs to the encoders feature dimension to predict the representations at + . The action generator follows Isaac-GR00T (Bjorck et al., 2025), using 16 DiT blocks of width 1,536 with alternating cross-attention and self-attention. It generates the action chunk from Gaussian noise, conditioned on the predictors full sequence of output hidden states. D.7 Policy Model Training Data We describe the datasets used to fine-tune LaLa-Policy in Section 5. The episode counts below refer to the data before the training/validation split. LIBERO. We use the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites of LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), comprising 40 language-conditioned manipulation tasks. The original data contain 50 human demonstrations per task, for total of 2,000 episodes. We adopt the replayed datasets released by Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., 2026).6 Its preprocessing removes no-op transitions and filters unsuccessful replays from the policy demonstration set. The resulting set contains 1,700 successful episodes: 430, 456, 438, and 376 from Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long, respectively. We use these episodes for policy training and the full set of 2,000 replays, including failures, for actionconditioned future prediction. RoboCasa. We use 24 kitchen manipulation tasks from RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024) under two data settings. For the setting with approximately 50 human demonstrations per task, we use the Cosmos Policy release.7 It provides 1,199 successful episodes for policy training and 1,291 replay episodes, including 92 failures, for action-conditioned future prediction. For the 300-demonstration setting, we use RoboCasas released data generated with MimicGen (Mandlekar et al., 2023). 5https://huggingface.co/nyu-visionx/RAEv2-models/tree/main/stage1/general/ dinov3l-k7 6https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/LIBERO-Cosmos-Policy 7https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/RoboCasa-Cosmos-Policy 31 D.8 LaLa-Policy Fine-tuning Details We initialize the predictor from pretrained LaLa-World and jointly train it with the newly added policy modules, while keeping the observation encoder frozen. The action generator is trained from scratch. We minimize flow-matching velocity loss on policy examples and mean squared error loss on future representations for both types of examples. Both loss coefficients are set to 1. We use AdamW with an effective global batch size of 256, (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.98), and weight decay of 0.05. The learning rate increases linearly from 1 106 to 1 104 over the first 1,000 optimizer steps, then follows cosine decay to 1 106. We clip the gradient norm at 1.0 and use bfloat16 mixed precision on eight NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs, with gradient accumulation to maintain the global batch size. We train for 8 epochs on LIBERO, 12 epochs on RoboCasa with approximately 50 human demonstrations per task, and 3 epochs on RoboCasa with 300 MimicGen demonstrations per task. D.9 Policy Model Evaluation Details We evaluate LaLa-Policy through direct interaction with the LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) and RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024) simulators, following the evaluation procedure of Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., 2026). The policy receives the task instruction, current proprioceptive state, and camera observations. LIBERO provides an external camera view and wrist view, while RoboCasa provides left and right external views and wrist view. After 10 initial no-op steps, the policy predicts an action chunk. On LIBERO, the chunk contains 16 actions, all of which are executed before the next query. On RoboCasa, the chunk contains 32 actions, of which we execute the first 16. Each subsequent query uses the latest simulator observations. The predicted future representations are not used for action selection during evaluation. We run 50 episodes for each of the 40 tasks across LIBEROs Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites. For RoboCasa, we run 50 episodes for each of 24 tasks, distributed equally across five test scenes with held-out object instances from split B. The step budgets follow the Cosmos Policy evaluation code: 220, 280, 300, and 520 for the four LIBERO suites, and 3001,000 depending on the RoboCasa task. An episode ends upon task success or exhaustion of its step budget. We report success rates averaged across suites for LIBERO and across tasks for RoboCasa.
